name: Single-family home (production)
summary: Production/spec detached homes. Cost is driven by finished floor area, finish level and region; framing, MEP rough-ins and interior finishes are ~60% of construction cost. The data is strong: NAHB's biennial Cost of Constructing a Home survey gives a full dollar breakdown, and Census Survey of Construction gives national medians for size and price per SF. The two disagree. NAHB's builder sample is not representative and runs higher than the large-builder Census medians, so the default sits between them.

typicalSize.method: Homes per subdivision phase or project. A judgment from typical production-builder phases, not sourced. Small infill builders do 5–20 lots; national builders run 100–300-lot communities in phases.

sfPerPrimaryUnit.method: Finished floor area per home. Mid sits between the Census 2025 built-for-sale median (2,216 SF) and average (2,427 SF) per e5. High ≈ NAHB 2024 survey home (2,647 SF, e2). Low ≈ entry-level product; per Census, 32% of 2025 completions were under 1,800 SF.

primaryUnitsPerAcre.method: Gross density incl. streets and open space. Census reports 41% of 2025 for-sale homes on lots under 7,000 SF (e12), i.e. 6.2 lots/net acre. Applying ~25–30% for ROW and open space gives ~4.5 gross. Larger NAHB-sample lots (20,907 SF avg, e12) imply ~1.5–2/acre, so the low is for suburban/rural product.

parkingPerPrimaryUnit.method: Attached 2-car garage is standard on production homes. Garage area is excluded from finished SF but its cost is inside the hard cost (NAHB categories include garage doors).

perPrimaryUnit.method: = perSF × sfPerPrimaryUnit: mid $145 × 2,300 SF ≈ $335k; low $115 × 1,900 ≈ $220k; high $190 × 2,700 ≈ $510k. Cross-check: NAHB 2024 construction cost $428,215 (e1), less permit, impact and water/sewer fees and A&E ($26,747), = $401,468 for a 2,647 SF home. That is direct builder cost before builder overhead, so with ~8–10% overhead it lands at the high end of this range.

perSF.method: Two primary national anchors. (1) NAHB 2024 survey: $162/SF construction cost (e2); net of permit/impact/utility fees and A&E (6.25%) = $152/SF of builder direct cost. (2) Census 2025 detached spec homes: median sale price $153.65/SF excluding lot (e4). Times the NAHB construction share of non-lot price (64.4% / 86.3% = 0.746) and net of fees (×0.9375), that is ≈ $107/SF of direct cost. The NAHB sample is not representative and skews to smaller builders (NAHB says so in e2), so the midpoint of the two anchors ($130) is used. That gets ~10% for general conditions/OH&P to express a contractor price, giving ≈ $143, rounded to $145. Low $115 ≈ Census-implied large-builder cost with minimal markup, South/Midwest. High $190 sits between NAHB + 12% OH&P ($170) and the Census average contractor-built contract price ($198, e6), for high-cost metros. 2024 and 2025 evidence is mixed (≤1 year gap), so the range is labeled 2025. Regional evidence (WA $309, e7) and the consumer-site average (Fixr $203, e8) are kept as spread indicators, not defaults.

scope.notes: Vertical house plus on-lot work: excavation and backfill, driveway, landscaping, flatwork, patio/deck, clean-up (NAHB stages II and VII). Includes contractor/builder general conditions and OH&P. Excludes land and horizontal lot development (streets and subdivision utilities; see the optional line item), permit, impact and water/sewer tap fees, A&E, builder G&A, marketing, commissions, financing and profit. Standard kitchen appliances are inside the hard cost, as NAHB includes them in construction cost.

qualityTiers.method: Economy ≈ low/mid of the per-SF range (115/145). Premium ≈ the Census 2025 contractor-built average ($198/SF, e6) relative to the detached spec median ($153.65, e4), a ×1.29 premium, rounded to 1.25. Luxury 1.6 is a judgment for semi-custom production at $230+/SF. For true one-off custom homes use the custom-home type.

systemSplit.method: Mapped from the NAHB 2024 Table 1 dollar breakdown (e3), excluding permit/impact/water-sewer fees and A&E ($401,468 direct). Then a 10% GC/OH&P markup was added to Div 01. Mapping: excavation/foundation/concrete 80% → 03 and 20% → 31; site-work 'other' → 31; framing, trusses, sheathing and half of interior trim/doors → 06; general metal → 05; exterior wall finish 25% → 04 (veneer) and 75% → 07, plus roofing and insulation → 07; windows/doors plus half of interior doors → 08; drywall, paint, flooring → 09; fireplace → 10; appliances → 11; cabinets/countertops → 12; plumbing plus fixtures → 22; HVAC → 23; electrical plus lighting → 26; landscaping, outdoor structures, driveway → 32; clean-up and 'other' → 01. The 04/07 and 03/31 allocations are assumptions.

lineItems.name: Horizontal lot development (streets, subdivision utilities, storm) per lot

cost.method: NAHB 2024 finished lot cost $91,057 per home (e1) includes raw land plus development. Assumes development is ~45–65% of the finished-lot figure on greenfield suburban lots, so mid ≈ $50k. Low/high reflect small infill lots versus large lots with long utility runs. Verify against local lot-development budgets.

lineItems.notes: Turn on when buying raw or entitled land instead of finished lots. Off-site and over-sizing improvements are extra.

lineItems.name: On-site septic system (3-bedroom)

cost.method: Fixr range for a 3-bedroom septic system (e11). Mid ≈ midpoint.

lineItems.notes: Census: 9% of 2025 for-sale homes used septic. Only for lots without public sewer.

cost.method: Fixr well drilling range (e11). Mid is a judgment toward the lower half, as most wells are shallow-to-moderate depth.

lineItems.name: Kitchen appliance package

cost.method: Mid = NAHB 2024 appliances line ($7,499, e3). Low/high is a judgment for builder-grade versus upgraded packages.

lineItems.notes: Already inside the hard cost; shown as a carve-out.

lineItems.name: Landscaping, driveway and outdoor structures (on-lot)

cost.method: Mid = NAHB 2024 landscaping ($9,269) + outdoor structures ($4,722) + driveway ($9,635) per e3. Low/high is a judgment.

lineItems.notes: Already inside the hard cost; shown as a carve-out.

pctOfHard.method: From NAHB 2024 (e9, e10), as a % of the $401,468 direct construction cost: A&E $6,480 (1.6%); permit $7,640 + impact $6,367 + water/sewer $6,260 = $20,267 (5.0%); construction financing $10,220 (2.5%); builder overhead and G&A $38,248 (9.5%); marketing $5,633 (1.4%). Total 20.1%, used as the mid. Sales commission ($18,955, 4.7%) and builder profit (11% of price) are excluded. Low assumes low-fee jurisdictions and a lean overhead structure. High covers high-impact-fee jurisdictions (CA, WA) plus commissions.

softCosts.notes: NAHB 2024 per-home fees: building permit $7,640, impact fee $6,367, water and sewer fees/inspections $6,260 (e10). Add sales commissions (~2.8% of sales price) for for-sale product.

design.method: Production builders reuse permitted plans, so design contingency is minimal. A judgment based on standard practice; no source found.

hard.method: Typical builder/lender hard-cost contingency for repeat production product. A judgment; no type-specific source found.

soft.method: General development norm; no type-specific source found.

perPrimaryUnit.method: Hard low $220k × (1 + 14% soft) ≈ $250k, less ~20% for small entry-level homes in low-cost markets ≈ $200k. High $510k × 1.28 ≈ $650k, plus headroom for high-cost metros ≈ $750k. Excludes land and lot development.

openQuestions: Public builder 10-K 'stick and brick' cost per SF (e.g., large national builders) would give a direct large-production cost anchor below the NAHB survey.
Lot development cost per lot is derived. A Zonda/John Burns or municipal lot-development benchmark would replace it.
The NAHB 2026 Construction Cost Survey (expected early 2027) should replace the 2024 figures.
